content:
NASA team dates Sahara meteorite to at least 4.1 billion years.

Offering a rare glimpse into the earliest geological history of Mars, NASA-funded researchers Oct. 29 reported that a meteorite discovered in the Sahara Desert had formed at least 4.1 billion years ago, preserving evidence of the Red Planet's ancient crust and its interactions with water during the earliest stages of planetary development.

Believed to have formed approximately 4.5 billion years ago, Mars has undergone extensive geological and environmental changes, with evidence from orbiters, landers, and rovers indicating that liquid water once existed across portions of a planet now characterized by a cold, dry surface and thin atmosphere.

Much of what scientists have learned about that history has come from spacecraft observations, but Martian meteorites recovered on Earth have provided another means of examining the planet's composition.

Ejected from Mars by asteroid impacts before eventually falling to Earth, these meteorites represent fragments of the planet's geological history, although most known specimens formed considerably later than the ancient crust that covers much of its surface.

One particularly unusual specimen emerged in 2022, when prospectors recovered a collection of rose-colored rocks weighing approximately 800 grams (1.76 pounds) from the Sahara Desert in Mali, near the Teghaza salt plain from which the meteorite eventually received its name.

Initially identified as Martian by researchers at the University of New Mexico, Teghaza 001 displayed oxygen isotope signatures consistent with other meteorites from the Red Planet, but its unusual mineral composition and texture suggested that the rock differed from previously studied specimens.

Further investigation involved scientists from NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), the California Institute of Technology, the University of California, Los Angeles, the University of New Mexico, and the University of Maine, who examined the meteorite to determine its age, geological origin, and evidence of changes after its formation.

Published in the scientific journal Science in October, the study established Teghaza 001 as one of the three oldest Martian meteorites ever identified, with its distinctive mixture of minerals providing evidence of ancient crust that formed as molten rock cooled before undergoing subsequent alteration by water.

"It was only after we started looking closely that we realized this meteorite is really unique," said Yang Liu, the study's lead author and a planetary scientist at JPL. "One of the paper's reviewers called it a Rosetta Stone for Mars."

Unlike other ancient Martian meteorites, including ALH84001 and the fragment-rich specimen known as Black Beauty, Teghaza 001 consisted of a single type of igneous rock containing minerals that preserved evidence of both its original formation and later geological changes.

Among those minerals were tiny zircon crystals, which contain radioactive elements that decay at predictable rates, allowing scientists to estimate when a rock formed by measuring the proportions of those elements and their decay products.

Using uranium-lead dating of the zircon crystals alongside another technique that measured rubidium and strontium isotopes within individual mineral grains, the researchers determined that Teghaza 001 had formed at least 4.1 billion years ago.

Developed through research involving Caltech scientist François Tissot and University of Maine professor Alicia Cruz-Uribe, the rubidium-strontium method allowed scientists to analyze individual grains using a laser and highly sensitive laboratory instruments, preserving most of the rare meteorite rather than dissolving an entire sample for testing.

"Right now, we are one of very few labs in the world able to perform this kind of age-dating, and the first to date such an ancient Martian meteorite," Tissot explained. "Our hope is to pave the way for dating even more Martian meteorites, or samples returned from other planets, their moons, and asteroids."

A color-enhanced microscopic image of Teghaza 001 distinguishes mineral grains within the meteorite, whose composition helped researchers reconstruct Mars' ancient geological history.

Evidence of ancient Martian water

Beyond establishing its age, the mineral measurements revealed that Teghaza 001 had interacted with Martian water approximately 4.1 billion years ago, indicating that the rock itself could have formed even earlier.

Additional evidence emerged from the meteorite's oxygen isotopes, chemical composition, and minerals altered by water, which together suggested that fluids had moved through portions of Mars' early crust and interacted with rocks formed from cooling magma.

A separate study published in Science Advances in June examined hydrogen isotopes preserved in Teghaza 001, finding chemical evidence that ancient Martian water had already been affected by the loss of hydrogen from the planet's atmosphere more than 4 billion years ago.

"This is really our first piece of Martian crust from a part of Mars we've never had a sample of before," said Lee Saper, the study's second author, who conducted the research while at JPL before joining NASA's Ames Research Center. "It records interactions of water and rock and maybe even an imprint of the Martian atmosphere as it was losing water."

Seeking to identify where the meteorite might have originated, researchers also compared its mineralogy and chemistry with observations collected by NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, identifying 13 locations with potentially matching geological characteristics.

Several of those locations fell within the heavily cratered southern highlands of Mars, where ancient terrain preserved evidence of geological processes dating to the planet's early development, although the scientists could not determine the meteorite's exact point of origin.

While the findings did not establish whether Mars once supported life, the evidence of ancient water-rock interactions added to researchers' understanding of environmental conditions during a period when the planet's crust and atmosphere were still developing.

With Teghaza 001 providing a previously unavailable sample of that early history, further examination of its minerals could help scientists investigate how Mars formed, how water moved through its ancient crust, and how the planet evolved toward the colder, drier conditions observed today.
